ourClaims.studySummary: A meta-analysis of 9 RCTs (Kongkeaw et al., 2014) found Bacopa significantly improved attention, cognitive processing, and working memory versus placebo. Effects are cumulative — most studies measure outcomes at 8–12 weeks. Best evidence is for memory consolidation rather than acute recall.

humanEffects.notes: Meta-analysis of 9 RCTs confirms effects on new memory formation; long-term recall improves more than immediate recall.
Significant in anxious populations; more modest in healthy low-stress subjects.
Improvements are modest acutely; significant when measured at 12-week mark.
Some studies show initial slowing of processing speed before 6 weeks — this is a known temporary effect that reverses.

sideEffects: GI discomfort at high doses (take with food)

howToTake.timing: With your largest meal of the day — morning or evening both work
howToTake.withFood: Bacosides are fat-soluble. Taking Bacopa with food (especially a meal with dietary fat) improves bioavailability significantly. Do not take on an empty stomach.
howToTake.forms: Capsule is most practical. Powder has a bitter, unpleasant taste. Look for standardisation to at least 40–55% bacosides on the label — unstandardised herbal products may contain very little active compound.

studies.title: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on cognitive effects of Bacopa monnieri extract.
studies.population: healthy and clinical adults, chronic dosing ≥12 weeks, no co-medication
studies.dose: not uniform across pooled trials; range not stated in abstract
studies.outcome: Trail Making Test B, choice reaction time (speed of attention)
studies.result: Trail B shortened by 17.9ms (95% CI -24.6 to -11.2, p<0.001); choice reaction time improved 10.6ms (95% CI -12.1 to -9.2, p<0.001)

studies.title: Effects of a standardized Bacopa monnieri extract on cognitive performance, anxiety, and depression in the elderly: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
studies.journal: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
studies.population: healthy elderly, mean age 73.5, no clinical dementia
studies.outcome: AVLT delayed recall (primary); Stroop; STAI anxiety; CESD-10 depression
studies.result: Bacopa improved AVLT delayed recall and Stroop vs placebo; anxiety (STAI) and depression (CESD-10) decreased in Bacopa group but increased in placebo (significant between-group difference); no effect on divided attention or WAIS digit task
studies.fundingConflict: NIH-supported (Research Support, N.I.H., Extramural per MeSH)

studies.title: Does Bacopa monnieri improve memory performance in older persons? Results of a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial.
studies.journal: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
studies.outcome: Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (AVLT) verbal learning and delayed recall
studies.result: Significant improvement in verbal learning, acquisition and delayed recall (AVLT trials p=0.000 to 0.048); CFT, MAC-Q, TMT improved but not significantly

studies.title: An acute, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study of 320 mg and 640 mg doses of a special extract of Bacopa monnieri (CDRI 08) on sustained cognitive performance.
studies.outcome: Cognitive Demand Battery performance across repetitions
studies.result: 320mg dose improved performance at 1st, 2nd and 4th post-dose repetitions; no effect on cardiovascular measures or stress/fatigue ratings

studies.title: The Effects of a Bacopa monnieri Extract (Bacumen) on Cognition, Stress, and Fatigue in Healthy Adults: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
studies.outcome: verbal learning, attention, working memory (primary); self-reported stress/fatigue (secondary)
studies.result: No significant between-group difference on primary cognitive outcomes (verbal learning p=0.391, attention p=0.713, working memory p=0.610); significant reduction in self-reported stress reactivity (p=0.03) and task-induced fatigue; higher rate of self-reported adverse reactions in Bacopa group (p=0.024), mainly digestive complaints and headaches
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; registered ANZCTR-ACTRN12623000475640

studies.title: Comparative effects of Bacopa monnieri and Ginkgo biloba on cognitive functions: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
studies.dose: high-dose Bacopa defined as ≥600mg/day vs low-dose 300 to <600mg/day
studies.outcome: working memory, short-term memory, delayed memory, attention, processing speed (network meta-analysis, SMD)
studies.result: High-dose Bacopa (≥600mg/day) significantly outperformed low-dose Bacopa, both Ginkgo doses and placebo on working memory (SMD 1.84-2.04, all significant); no significant differences in sustained/selective attention or processing speed
studies.fundingConflict: Thailand Research Fund grant disclosed; registered PROSPERO CRD420251034900

verdicts.claim: Memory Consolidation — strong evidence, moderate magnitude, 9 studies
verdicts.reason: Directly traceable to Kongkeaw 2014 (9-RCT meta-analysis, n=518) showing significant cognitive/speed-of-attention gains, reinforced by two independent positive 12-week elderly RCTs (Calabrese 2008, Morgan & Stevens 2010) on delayed recall.

verdicts.claim: Anxiety Reduction — moderate evidence, moderate magnitude, 5 studies
verdicts.reason: Calabrese 2008 found a significant between-group divergence in STAI anxiety scores over 12 weeks (Bacopa group improved, placebo worsened), consistent with the claimed 'moderate' strength.

verdicts.claim: Attention — moderate evidence, small magnitude, 6 studies
verdicts.reason: The most recent and largest single RCT in this space (Lopresti 2025, n=87 completers) found no significant effect on attention (p=0.713), contradicting the 'moderate' strength label; the positive attention signal in the literature rests mainly on the older Kongkeaw 2014 pooled speed-of-attention metric, not a replicated dedicated attention endpoint.

verdicts.claim: Processing Speed — mixed evidence, small magnitude, 4 studies, transient initial slowing
verdicts.reason: Correctly characterized as mixed; this matches the literature's well-documented transient 'Bacopa fog' pattern and low-powered small trials.

doseAssessment.trialRange: Most positive 12-week RCTs used 300mg/day of a standardized extract (BacoMind, unbranded 55% bacoside extracts); the 2026 network meta-analysis found ≥600mg/day superior to 300-450mg/day for working memory specifically.
doseAssessment.suggestedText: Our stated 300–450mg/day range sits within the classic trial dose used in the positive 2008-2010 elderly RCTs, but a 2026 network meta-analysis (29 RCTs, n=2107) found doses ≥600mg/day produced significantly larger working-memory effects than 300-450mg/day. Consider flagging that higher-dose formulations are an emerging area of evidence rather than the established standard.

safetySignals.signal: GI side effects (increased stool frequency, abdominal cramps, nausea) reported in a 12-week RCT in healthy older adults
Higher rate of self-reported adverse reactions (digestive complaints, headaches) vs placebo in a 2025 12-week RCT (p=0.024)

gaps: No dedicated human RCT data found on Bacopa use during pregnancy to substantiate the page's pregnancy caution (mechanistically plausible but not directly evidenced in the studies reviewed here).
Most positive trials are 12 weeks or shorter; long-term (>12 week) continuous-use safety/efficacy data is thin, despite the page's FAQ claiming long-term use is well supported.

The newest, best-designed RCT (Lopresti 2025) failed to replicate primary cognitive benefits at 300mg/day, creating tension with the page's confident 'strong evidence' framing for memory that isn't fully reconciled in current literature.
No drug-interaction studies located for Bacopa (e.g., with thyroid medication, anticholinergics).
